summaryEn: Seventy years of transformers and switchgear, suddenly in demand from two directions at once — Taiwan's grid hardening programme and America's AI data centres. Earnings and dividends have both roughly doubled in four years; last quarter's record profit came with negative operating cash flow.
model: editorial (truth-audited: FinMind + press; heavy-electrical framing — the 66% revenue share from heavy electrical, the NT$9.4bn Taipower tender win, 30–40% capacity expansion, Mitsubishi Electric cooperation opening the US data centre supply chain and 300+ MWh of storage projects credited, but a 28.39× multiple on 9.37% ROE, project-driven margin swings, and 2026Q1 operating cash flow of −NT$1.33bn against a record NT$1.52bn net profit all stated plainly; sector 電機機械 → Heavy Electrical & Green Energy)

sections.bodyMarkdown:
Shihlin Electric & Engineering (士林電機廠, TWSE: 1503) has made the equipment that moves electricity since **1955**. Founded seven years after Taiwan Power began electrifying the island and **listed in December 1969**, it builds **transformers, gas-insulated switchgear, distribution panels and high- and low-voltage switching equipment** — the machinery between a power station and a factory. **Heavy electrical products are 66% of revenue.**

For most of seventy years this was a stable, unexciting business tracking Taiwanese infrastructure spending. It is not stable now, because **two demand shocks arrived at once**.

The first is domestic. Taiwan is running a **grid resilience programme** to harden an electricity network that has suffered high-profile failures, and in **February 2026 Taipower released a tender worth about NT$9.4bn** focused on **transformers and gas-insulated switchgear** — with Shihlin among the winners. The second is foreign and larger: **AI data centres in the United States** need enormous quantities of exactly this equipment, and Shihlin has entered that supply chain through **technical cooperation with Mitsubishi Electric**. Alongside both, it expects to win **more than 300 MWh of behind-the-meter energy storage projects in 2026**.

Capacity is being built for it: **large power transformers entered production in 2025Q2 and medium distribution transformers follow in 2026, lifting capacity 30–40%**.

The results have followed. Annual EPS ran **NT$3.86 (FY2022) → 4.51 → 5.82 (FY2024) → NT$6.28 (FY2025)**, and **2026Q1 delivered NT$2.79, up 19%** on a year earlier — with gross margin at **23.8%** and operating margin at **16.1%**, both near the top of their recent range. Dividends have risen from **NT$1.8 (FY2021) to NT$5.0 (FY2025)**. **Trailing return on equity is 9.37%.**

Three things need stating plainly. **The valuation is demanding**: at **NT$190.50 the shares trade at 28.4× earnings and 2.61× book** — a growth multiple on a **9.37% return on equity**. **The quarterly numbers swing hard** because this is a project business: gross margin has ranged **17.2% to 23.8%** and operating margin **6.6% to 16.1%** within six quarters, and monthly revenue ran **+35%, +33%, then −11%**. And most specifically: **2026Q1's record NT$1.52bn of net profit came with operating cash flow of −NT$1.33bn** — a NT$2.8bn divergence, consistent with working capital building ahead of a capacity expansion, but a gap that needs to close.

The honest read: **a seventy-year-old equipment maker with two genuine demand drivers and real capacity being added — priced for the growth, and currently converting none of its record profit into cash.**

Shihlin Electric was founded in **1955**, in the early years of Taiwan's electrification. An economy building a power grid needs **transformers** — the machines that step voltage up for transmission and down again for use — along with **switchgear** to control and protect the network, and distribution equipment to deliver it. These are heavy, long-lived, safety-critical products, and a country that intends to industrialise needs to make them itself or buy them permanently from abroad. Taiwan chose to make them. The company **listed in 1969**.

For decades the business was straightforward and slow: sell equipment to **Taiwan Power**, to industrial plants, to construction projects, at margins set by competitive tendering. Shihlin diversified along the way into motors, elevators, industrial automation and later **electric vehicle charging** and **energy storage**, but the core remained heavy electrical equipment — **66% of revenue** today.

The transformation was not something Shihlin did. **The world changed around the transformer.**

Two forces arrived together. First, **electricity grids everywhere are being rebuilt** — for renewables, for resilience, for electrification of transport and heating — after decades of underinvestment. In Taiwan specifically, high-profile grid failures produced a national **grid resilience programme**, and **Taipower's February 2026 tender of about NT$9.4bn** for transformers and gas-insulated switchgear is one visible instalment. Second, **AI data centres** began demanding power at a scale that overwhelmed the world's transformer and switchgear manufacturing capacity, with lead times stretching to years. Shihlin entered that market through **technical cooperation with Mitsubishi Electric**, which gave it both the product credibility and the route into the **US supply chain**.

The company's response has been to build: **large power transformers into production from 2025Q2, medium distribution transformers in 2026, capacity up 30–40%**. It is an unusual position for a seventy-year-old industrial company — the product did not change, the world's need for it did.

- **1955 (3 Nov)** — Shihlin Electric & Engineering founded, making transformers and electrical equipment for Taiwan's electrification.
- **1969 (15 Dec)** — **Lists on the Taiwan Stock Exchange (1503)**.
- **1970s–2010s** — Builds out heavy electrical equipment — transformers, switchgear, distribution panels — alongside motors, elevators and industrial automation; heavy electrical becomes **66% of revenue**.
- **2020s** — Diversifies into **EV charging** and **energy storage** as Taiwan's energy mix changes.
- **2022** — **FY2022 EPS NT$3.86**; dividend **NT$2.0**.
- **2023** — **FY2023 EPS NT$4.51**; dividend raised sharply to **NT$3.0**.
- **2024** — **FY2024 EPS NT$5.82**; dividend **NT$4.5**. Grid investment and data centre demand accelerate.
- **2025Q2** — **Large power transformers enter production**, the first step of a capacity expansion of **30–40%**.
- **2025** — **FY2025 EPS NT$6.28**; dividend **NT$5.0**. Enters the **US data centre supply chain** through **technical cooperation with Mitsubishi Electric**.
- **2026 (February)** — **Taipower releases a tender of about NT$9.4bn** for transformers and gas-insulated switchgear under its grid resilience programme; **Shihlin is among the winners**.
- **2026Q1** — **Record quarter: EPS NT$2.79 (+19%)**, net profit **NT$1.52bn**, gross margin **23.8%**, operating margin **16.1%**. **Operating cash flow of −NT$1.33bn.** Medium distribution transformers due into production during the year; **300+ MWh of behind-the-meter storage projects expected in 2026**.

Shihlin's accounts show **a project-driven equipment maker in a genuine upcycle, with a cash-flow question attached to its best quarter**.

- **Earnings have grown consistently.** Annual EPS: **NT$3.86 (FY2022) → 4.51 (FY2023) → 5.82 (FY2024) → NT$6.28 (FY2025)** — a **63% increase in three years** — and **2026Q1's NT$2.79 was up 19%** on the prior year, the best quarter in the record.
- **Margins swing with project timing.** Gross margin: **18.1% (2024Q4) → 23.6% → 22.9% → 19.8% → 17.2% (2025Q4) → 23.8% (2026Q1)**. Operating margin: **6.6% → 16.1%**, dipping to 7.0% in between. This is normal for a business recognising revenue on large equipment contracts, and it means **no single quarter describes the company** — the annual figures do.
- **The cash-flow gap in the record quarter.** **2026Q1 produced NT$1.52bn of net profit and −NT$1.33bn of operating cash flow** — a divergence of nearly **NT$2.9bn**. In a business expanding capacity **30–40%** and building inventory against a growing order book, working capital absorption of this kind is explicable. It is also the single most important number to watch: **profit that does not become cash is not yet profit.**
- **Return on equity is modest.** **9.37% trailing**, on **NT$38.85bn of equity** — respectable for heavy electrical manufacturing, but well below what the share price implies.
- **A conservative balance sheet funding the expansion.** **NT$60.43bn of assets** on **NT$38.85bn of equity** — a **35.7% debt ratio** — with **NT$3.26bn of cash**. There is ample capacity to fund the transformer capacity build.
- **A dividend that has nearly tripled.** Cash dividends (FinMind, by fiscal year): **NT$1.6 (2019, 2020) → 1.8 (2021) → 2.0 (2022) → 3.0 (2023) → 4.5 (2024) → NT$5.0 (2025)**. The **2.62% yield** at NT$190.50 is modest because the share price has risen faster than the payout.
- **The valuation is the crux.** **28.4× earnings and 2.61× book** for a company earning **9.37% on equity**. That multiple prices the Taipower programme, the US data centre pipeline and the capacity expansion as though they are already in the results.

The financing reality: **genuine, sustained earnings growth funded from a strong balance sheet — with a record quarter that generated no cash and a share price that has already discounted several years of good news.**

**Stance: a seventy-year-old transformer maker with two real demand shocks — Taiwan's grid programme and US AI data centres — growing earnings 63% in three years, at 28.4x earnings on a 9.37% return on equity.**

The bull case:

1. **Two independent demand drivers, both verified.** Domestically, **Taipower's February 2026 tender of about NT$9.4bn** for transformers and gas-insulated switchgear under the grid resilience programme, with Shihlin among the winners. Internationally, the **US data centre supply chain**, entered through **technical cooperation with Mitsubishi Electric**.
2. **Capacity being added into a global shortage.** **Large power transformers in production from 2025Q2**, medium distribution transformers in 2026, **capacity up 30–40%**. Transformer lead times worldwide have stretched to years — capacity is the binding constraint on the whole industry.
3. **The results are already there.** EPS **NT$3.86 → NT$6.28** in three years, **2026Q1 up 19%** to a record, gross margin at **23.8%** and operating margin at **16.1%**, both near the top of their range.
4. **A green-energy second leg.** More than **300 MWh of behind-the-meter storage projects** expected in 2026, plus EV charging.
5. **Balance sheet strength.** **35.7% debt ratio** and **NT$38.85bn of equity** — the expansion is comfortably funded.

The counter-arguments:

- **The record quarter produced no cash.** **NT$1.52bn of net profit against −NT$1.33bn of operating cash flow.** Until that converges, the earnings quality is unproven.
- **The valuation.** **28.4× earnings and 2.61× book** on a **9.37% ROE**. This is a growth price for a manufacturer earning single-digit returns on a large capital base.
- **Project lumpiness makes results unreliable quarter to quarter.** Gross margin **17.2% to 23.8%**, operating margin **6.6% to 16.1%**, monthly revenue **+35%, +33%, then −11%**.
- **Demand is policy- and capex-dependent.** Taipower spending is budgeted; data centre construction depends on hyperscaler decisions.
- **Everyone is expanding.** Shihlin is one of several Taiwanese heavy-electrical firms adding transformer capacity into the same shortage.

A **shortage-capacity** thesis: real demand, real capacity, real earnings growth — bought at a price that already assumes several more years of it.

Shihlin makes **the equipment between the power station and the machine**:

- **Transformers (the core).** Step-up transformers for transmission and step-down units for distribution — large, heavy, long-lived machines built to specification for a substation, factory or data centre. Lead times are long, qualification matters, and a failure takes a facility offline, so buyers choose on reliability and track record rather than price alone.
- **Gas-insulated switchgear (GIS) and distribution equipment.** Switching and protection apparatus that isolates faults and routes power. GIS in particular is technically demanding and in global shortage — which is why it featured specifically in **Taipower's NT$9.4bn tender**.
- **The rest.** Motors, elevators, industrial automation, **EV charging** and **energy storage** — with **300+ MWh of behind-the-meter storage projects** expected in 2026. **Heavy electrical is 66% of revenue**; these are the balance.
- **How revenue and profit arise, and why quarters mislead.** Large equipment is sold on **contracts recognised over months**, so a quarter in which several units complete looks strong and a quarter of work-in-progress looks weak. That is why gross margin ranged **17.2% to 23.8%** and operating margin **6.6% to 16.1%** within six quarters, and why **monthly revenue ran +35%, +33%, then −11%**. Only annual figures describe the business.
- **Why capacity is the constraint.** Transformer manufacturing capacity worldwide is scarce, and building it takes years — factory space, presses, winding equipment, testing facilities and skilled labour. Shihlin's **30–40% expansion**, with **large power transformers from 2025Q2** and medium distribution transformers in 2026, is the company's answer to demand it cannot currently serve.
- **The Mitsubishi Electric relationship.** Technical cooperation that provides product credibility and, critically, **access to the US data centre supply chain** — a market Shihlin could not have entered alone on reputation.

The levers are **order intake, capacity utilisation, project execution and the mix between domestic grid work and export data centre work**. The strength is a scarce manufacturing capability meeting simultaneous domestic and international demand, funded from a **35.7% debt ratio**. The vulnerability is that **capacity expansion consumes working capital before it produces revenue** — which is precisely what **2026Q1's −NT$1.33bn of operating cash flow against NT$1.52bn of profit** reflects.

Electrical equipment has become one of the most supply-constrained industries in the world, for reasons that took decades to build up.

- **Why the shortage exists.** Grids in developed economies were built decades ago and underinvested in since. Simultaneously, **renewables require more grid connections, electrification raises load, and AI data centres demand power at unprecedented density**. Transformer and switchgear manufacturing capacity did not expand to meet any of it, and **global lead times have stretched to years**.
- **Why capacity cannot respond quickly.** A transformer factory requires specialised winding and pressing equipment, high-voltage testing facilities, and skilled labour that takes years to train. This is not a business where capacity appears in twelve months — which is why the shortage has persisted and why manufacturers can price accordingly.
- **Taiwan's specific programme.** Following high-profile grid failures, Taipower's **grid resilience programme** has generated a sustained pipeline of equipment orders. The **February 2026 tender of about NT$9.4bn** for transformers and GIS is one instalment, shared among Taiwan's heavy-electrical makers — **Shihlin, Fortune Electric (1519), Chung-Hsin Electric, Yaley** and others, a group Taiwanese media refer to collectively as the sector's leaders.
- **How Shihlin compares within that group.** **Fortune Electric (1519)**, elsewhere in this collection, is the more concentrated pure-play and has been valued accordingly — at a far higher price-to-book. **TECO (1504)**, also here, is broader and more diluted. **Shihlin sits between them**: heavy electrical is 66% of revenue, enough to matter but not the whole company.
- **The international dimension.** The **US data centre market** is the larger prize, and access requires credibility with buyers who have no history with Taiwanese suppliers. **Mitsubishi Electric cooperation** is how Shihlin obtained it — a route that also constrains, since the relationship shapes what and where it can sell.
- **The cycle risk.** Grid investment is **budgeted**, and data centre construction is **hyperscaler capital spending**. Both are currently strong; neither is permanent, and every manufacturer in the industry is expanding into the same shortage.

Shihlin's position is **genuinely advantaged by scarcity**. The industry truth is that **shortages end when capacity arrives** — and the entire industry is now building it.

**Strengths**
- **Seventy years in heavy electrical equipment**; **66% of revenue** from transformers, switchgear and distribution equipment.
- **Two verified demand drivers**: Taipower's grid resilience programme (**NT$9.4bn February 2026 tender**, Shihlin among winners) and the **US data centre supply chain** via **Mitsubishi Electric** cooperation.
- **Capacity expansion of 30–40%**: large power transformers from 2025Q2, medium distribution transformers in 2026.
- **EPS up 63% in three years** (NT$3.86 → NT$6.28); dividend **NT$1.8 → NT$5.0**; **35.7% debt ratio**.

**Weaknesses**
- **2026Q1's record NT$1.52bn profit came with −NT$1.33bn of operating cash flow.**
- **Trailing ROE of only 9.37%** against a **28.4× earnings and 2.61× book** valuation.
- **Project lumpiness**: gross margin **17.2–23.8%**, operating margin **6.6–16.1%**, monthly revenue **+35% to −11%**.

**Opportunities**
- **300+ MWh of behind-the-meter storage projects** expected in 2026; EV charging.
- Global transformer and GIS shortage with multi-year lead times.
- Further US data centre orders as capacity comes online.

**Threats**
- **Industry-wide capacity expansion** eventually relieving the shortage.
- **Taipower budget** and **hyperscaler capex** both being external, policy- and cycle-driven.
- Working capital absorption during expansion; competition from Fortune Electric, Chung-Hsin and global majors.

- **The record quarter generated no cash (the most specific risk).** **2026Q1 reported NT$1.52bn of net profit and −NT$1.33bn of operating cash flow** — a divergence of nearly **NT$2.9bn**. A company expanding capacity **30–40%** while building inventory against a rising order book will absorb working capital, and this is the likely explanation. But **profit that does not convert to cash is not yet earned**, and if the gap persists across several quarters it becomes the central issue rather than a timing effect.
- **The valuation prices in the pipeline.** **28.4× earnings and 2.61× book** for a company earning **9.37% on equity**. The Taipower orders, the US data centre entry and the capacity expansion are all real — and all already reflected in the price. Execution merely meeting expectations may not be enough.
- **Project accounting makes quarters unreliable.** Gross margin between **17.2% and 23.8%** and operating margin between **6.6% and 16.1%** within six quarters, with monthly revenue swinging from **+35% to −11%**. Any single period, good or bad, will mislead.
- **Both demand drivers are external.** **Taipower spending is a government budget**; **US data centre construction is hyperscaler capital spending**. Neither is contracted indefinitely, and both can be deferred.
- **The shortage will end.** Transformer and switchgear scarcity is the reason margins and orders are strong. **Every manufacturer in the industry is expanding**, including Shihlin's Taiwanese competitors, and materials shortages historically resolve when capacity arrives.
- **The Mitsubishi relationship is an enabler and a dependency.** It provides US market credibility that Shihlin could not obtain alone — which also means the terms of that cooperation shape what it can sell and where.

Shihlin's outlook depends on **whether the new capacity converts a strong order book into cash-backed earnings.** The axes to watch:

- **Operating cash flow — the priority metric.** **−NT$1.33bn against NT$1.52bn of net profit in 2026Q1.** Convergence over the coming quarters would confirm the working-capital explanation; continued divergence would call the earnings quality into question regardless of how the income statement reads.
- **Capacity coming online and being filled.** **Large power transformers from 2025Q2**, medium distribution transformers during 2026, total capacity up **30–40%**. Utilisation of that capacity is what turns the shortage into profit.
- **Order intake from both sources.** Taipower's grid resilience tenders — following the **NT$9.4bn February 2026 award** — and **US data centre orders** through the **Mitsubishi Electric** channel. The second is the larger long-term opportunity and the one to watch for evidence.
- **Annual EPS, not quarterly.** **NT$3.86 → 4.51 → 5.82 → NT$6.28**, with **2026Q1 at NT$2.79**. Project accounting makes the full year the only meaningful measure.
- **Margin through the cycle.** Gross margin has ranged **17.2% to 23.8%**. Sustained levels near the top of that range would indicate the shortage is still supporting pricing.

Bottom line: Shihlin Electric has made **transformers and switchgear since 1955**, and now finds that equipment demanded simultaneously by **Taiwan's grid resilience programme** — including a **NT$9.4bn Taipower tender it won a share of** — and by **US AI data centres**, entered through **Mitsubishi Electric cooperation**, with **capacity rising 30–40%** and **300+ MWh of storage projects** expected in 2026. EPS has risen **63% in three years** and the dividend nearly tripled. It is also a company earning **9.37% on equity** while trading at **28.4× earnings**, whose **quarterly margins swing by six percentage points on project timing**, and whose **record quarter produced negative operating cash flow of NT$1.33bn**. Judge it on **operating cash flow and annual earnings** — genuine scarcity, genuinely priced.
